tool_items.content:
{"id":1008751744,"date":"2026-01-15T00:01:00","date_gmt":"2026-01-15T05:01:00","guid":{"rendered":"https://www.aei.org/?post_type=report&p=1008751744"},"modified":"2026-01-14T17:05:57","modified_gmt":"2026-01-14T22:05:57","slug":"the-looming-data-imperative-to-inform-agricultural-policy","status":"publish","type":"report","link":"https://www.aei.org/research-products/report/the-looming-data-imperative-to-inform-agricultural-policy/","title":{"rendered":"The Looming Data Imperative to Inform Agricultural Policy"},"content":{"rendered":"

Key Points

  • Recent staffing losses, budget shortfalls in purchasing power, and data cancellations will compromise the US Department of Agriculture’s capacity and capability to provide official statistics to track and monitor the US agricultural economy.
  • The consequences will worsen data quality and the supply of many products. But decisions still need to be made, and the vacuum will be filled using incomplete databases that will be poor substitutes for federal sources they replace. Additionally, government policymakers will have no oversight of the access and accountability of these data.
  • The opportunity is at hand to meet the future and design a sustainable direction to produce data and statistics that can inform policies and programs in the US agricultural economy.

Introduction

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) produces a bounty of data, official statistics, analyses, and forecasts on the US agricultural economy, households’ access to and consumption of food, farming activities intersecting with the environment, and the state of rural communities. These data products are gathered, compiled, and disseminated for use by the business community, citizens, government agencies, and nonprofits as they pursue their economic, social, and political objectives. These data are public goods—available to all data users simultaneously without affecting others’ ability to use the same data.

However, the USDA is facing an imminent threat to its ability to provide data to monitor the US agricultural sector and inform policy. This situation has been percolating for some time, with declining budgets and the USDA’s reliance on resource-straining methodologies, practices, and protocols for collecting and disseminating data that meet use requirements.

The first year of the second Trump administration has accelerated the threat with the cancellation of data collections and significant staff losses at USDA’s two official statistical agencies—the Economic Research Service (ERS) and the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS)—with no prospect of backfilling. ERS and NASS lost 27 percent and 40 percent of their staffs, respectively, during fiscal year (FY) 2025. Budget pressures were substantial as well. ERS and NASS budgets lost 9 percent and 12 percent of their purchasing power, respectively, between FY2021 and FY2025.1

Continuing a business-as-usual approach for producing and disseminating data and research outputs about the US agricultural economy is no longer sustainable. It would significantly impede the range of data collections and the data quality supporting research to inform policymakers and private-sector decision-makers.

Our data investments are strategic assets that can be leveraged to advance economic, social, and political objectives. Pertinent, quality data are the foundation for good analysis, which in turn supports sound policy. Bad data misinform analysis, which leads to misguided policy. And the absence of data is a precondition for preventing objective analysis, resulting in policy driven by self-serving anecdotes and narratives. The opportunity is at hand to reimagine how USDA meets these data needs as we enter the second quarter of the 21st century.

Data and USDA

Agricultural data collection goes back to 1790, and the first formal US agricultural census was conducted in 1840.2 Data are statistical products, defined as the

information dissemination products that are published or otherwise made available for public use that describe, estimate, forecast, or analyze the characteristics of groups, customarily without identifying the persons or organizations that comprise such groups or individual data observations with respect to those persons or organizations. Statistical products include general-purpose tabulations, analyses, projections, forecasts, or other statistical reports.3

USDA is a treasure trove of information. Central to USDA data collection are ERS and NASS, two of the 13 federal statistical agencies mandated to collect and disseminate official statistical products as their core function.4 Annually, NASS releases more than 400 statistical survey products and reports, and it functions as a data warehouse.5 ERS annually releases approximately 240 data products and 120 related reports and events.6

In addition, ERS works in tandem with NASS on several data collection efforts. Examples include the 2024 Tenure, Ownership, and Transition of Agricultural Land Survey sample of 40,000 landowners and 40,000 producers;7 the Agricultural Resource Management Survey,8 which has an annual sample size of approximately 30,000 farms and serves as the workhorse of much of ERS analysis on the farm economy; and the Crop Sequence Boundaries, which uses satellite imagery to produce estimates of field boundaries, crop acreage, and crop rotations across the contiguous United States.9 NASS is the data factory while ERS serves as the retail side of the USDA official data shop, producing an extensive set of outlook, research, and technical reports, as well as briefings and analyses for internal government use.

The monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) is a widely cited report addressing the commodity outlook nationally and globally, along with in-depth analysis. The WASDE releases are produced by the World Agricultural Outlook Board and are recognized as the benchmark for agricultural forecasts that farmers, agribusinesses, commodity analysts, and other stakeholders rely on. The World Agricultural Outlook Board coordinates a team of USDA experts from ERS and across the department who compose the Interagency Commodity Estimates Committee. Staffing losses have cut into the bench strength of this interagency team, affecting its ability to deliver its products. To the extent that the WASDE remains a high priority for USDA, staffing this report may require reassigning staff from other data products’ support and research activities or backfilling vacancies.

The other 16 USDA agencies collect data as by-products of their administration and implementation of a wide range of agricultural policy programs and services for farmers and ranchers. Some of these agencies include the Farm Service Agency, Risk Management Agency, Natural Resources Conservation Service, and Rural Housing Service. The confidential data, referred to as administrative data, are used for nonstatistical purposes. Nevertheless, the administrative data are valuable in research, as they are frequently blended with official statistical data to support many ERS reports and analyses. For example, the triannual Farm Income and Wealth Statistics forecast uses Farm Service Agency data,10 food safety research draws on the Food Safety and Inspection Service program data,11 and food- and nutrition-related research relies on Food and Nutrition Service program data.12

ERS and NASS strive to disseminate data products that are relevant to the policy and private-sector decision-making communities. Being relevant entails delivering timely data products. Since forecasts and projections have a short half-life, the current staffing shortages will affect the frequency and timeliness of data product releases.

The recent 43-day government shutdown offers a preview of the disrupted release of time-sensitive USDA data products. Highly anticipated forecasts and data releases that were delayed or skipped include the quarterly Outlook for US Agricultural Trade, which was released one month late; the monthly reports for WASDE and several other commodities, which were missed; and the third installment of the Farm Income and Wealth Statistics forecast, which had been scheduled for December 2025 but was skipped. Policymakers and the agricultural community must wait until early February for the next Farm Income and Wealth Statistics forecast release.

The Consequences of Fewer Data

John Maynard Keynes is often quoted as saying, “It is better to be roughly right than precisely wrong,”13 acknowledging two key factors in producing precision data products. The first is the need to balance timeliness and precision. Both are essential, but greater precision comes at a cost of delaying policy action and decision-making. The second factor is the recognition that social science research comes with an inherent measure of imprecision. Regarding agricultural data products, social science research dissects the consequences of decisions by input suppliers, farmers, commodity traders, food manufacturers and retailers, and consumers as they evaluate known and unknown trade-offs.

To better understand the nature of human decisions and their impact on society, we must first assemble the data that describe the factors that could influence the range of choices to investigate. From a policy-informing perspective, presenting the unbiased evolution of relevant historical data is a key starting point, allowing policymakers to track and monitor their policies’ impact on important outcomes. Examples of such outcomes include evaluating agricultural labor availability, mitigating adverse climatic events, and assessing and targeting the impact that food assistance programs have on alleviating food insecurity for vulnerable US households.

Failing to collect data amounts to flying blind, placing policy and private-sector decision-makers at a disadvantage. This loss in the supply of data is the first-order effect. The second-order effect follows from the demand for these data. Not providing data disadvantages policymakers, who need to track the landscape of businesses and households. Federal statistical agencies exercise the necessary delegated authorities mandated by federal law and the Office of Management and Budget to maintain trust in the data and analyses they provide to inform policymakers and private-sector decision-makers.14

Without trusted data, which provide an objective view of the decision landscape, alternative databases and other information disseminators will emerge. These nonfederal-sector efforts are more likely to be incomplete, not comparable across geographic or state boundaries, or released to private clients in advance while being inaccessible to the public. The one certainty is that national and state policymakers will have no oversight of the accessibility and accountability of these alternative data.

Going Forward

Behind the data products and analyses they generate is an army of subject matter experts, statisticians, and data scientists. These data products are rigorously reviewed by internal and external experts and frequently obtain input from external advisory committees.

Is there room for improvement? Certainly. All federal agencies collecting data have focused on continuous product improvements to produce more accurate measurements.15 The way federal statistical agencies such as NASS and ERS currently survey businesses and households is an expensive proposition. In-person surveys yield lower and lower response rates, resulting in increasing costs for data collection. Exploring the modernization of surveying approaches and processing is on the front burner for ERS, NASS, and other federal statistical agencies, and positive changes are certainly forthcoming.16

Challenges and Opportunities Outside of Government

ERS and NASS, along with the federal statistical system, are approaching a critical juncture as they work to modernize and adapt to a rapidly changing data landscape, driven by increasing demand for timely, detailed, and relevant information amid declining survey response rates and rising data-collection costs.

The current decentralized federal system has the advantage of providing deep subject matter expertise to data systems that are quickly accessible to inquiries. But the system faces challenges as it sustains and modernizes its data collection and dissemination and encourages agencies to coordinate with each other. Recent reports from the US Government Accountability Office and the American Statistical Association address the challenges facing federal statistical agencies, ERS and NASS included, as they adapt to modernization efforts and pivot away from relying so heavily on in-person surveying.17

At the same time, the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act mandates providing improved access to data and greater accountability for how data are deployed while safeguarding data providers’ confidentiality.18 In operational terms, the challenge entails how to harmonize the collaboration among official statistical agencies not only to reduce redundancies but also to leverage the system’s potential value and its wealth of data and expertise. In the face of these data infrastructure challenges, operating issues are magnified by depleted staffing.

Data users engage with ERS and NASS staff routinely in semiannual data-user conferences and informally through weekly inquiries to ERS and NASS staff. However, the NASS Advisory Committee on Agriculture Statistics, along with six other USDA advisory committees, was disbanded in May 2025.19 Shutting down this advisory committee closes the door to an important channel for user engagement and private-sector expertise in technologies and processes to support the modernization of data collection, curation, and dissemination.

How Should We Envision the Next Steps?

ERS and NASS are responsible for assembling the official national statistics for the US agricultural economy. Thus, a near-term strategy could focus on coordinating these agencies’ operational and strategic activities. Moving forward requires a clean-slate approach rather than trying to shoehorn one agency into the other. ERS and NASS have separate but complementary missions and goals. Economic subject matter expertise is the scarcest resource. ERS’s efforts build on the NASS data factory, but ERS also blends data from other federal statistical agencies such as the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the Energy Information Administration. A first step would be to leverage synergies in staffing, processes, and infrastructure modernization.

ERS and NASS recognize the need to respond to these emergent challenges. Farmers have consistently complained about USDA asking them the same questions in different applications and official statistical surveys. Both agencies are working through the bureaucratic maze to minimize redundancies in reporting and are collaborating with the Risk Management Agency and Farm Service Agency to access the surveyed farmers’ contracts for similar information. And both agencies have experimented with new processes and tools to lower the barriers to access data-instituting processes and tools, making data more accessible to empower decision-makers to make informed decisions and act based on data. The promise of artificial intelligence tools is on the horizon with chatbots being piloted to assist data users in accessing information by acting as a concierge service.

Proceeding with business as usual is simply unsustainable. Clearly, ERS and NASS do not have the budgetary or staffing support to continue current activities and modernize simultaneously. A necessary first step in conceptualizing the forward-looking US agricultural data system requires revisiting a data product’s value proposition to not only private and public data users but also data providers.

In this sense, a local-national-local perspective is key: Local data providers volunteer their information, which is aggregated to the regional and national level and then fed back to the local stakeholders—farmers, extension professionals, and local government decision-makers. In addition to being mindful of local stakeholders, response rates can improve as farmers see how their feedback is used to benefit their own businesses and the public. Recent ERS and NASS administrators have recognized this challenge, but it is imperative that this become a top priority.

Partnering for Data

A federal statistical agency’s ultimate role is to provide data that are objective, free of political influence, and can be trusted by the public. This entails setting a clear expectation that the data are suitable and sufficient for their intended use in policymaking, planning, and operational decision-making. Does providing the imprimatur on the official data product necessarily require the federal statistical agency to control all aspects of data collection, curation, and dissemination? As agencies explore more opportunities to blend public and private data, trust metrics need to be developed to convey that the data are fit for purpose—that is, the data conform to their use requirements. We need to move strategically toward blending private data with public data while maintaining confidentiality.

Opportunities exist to explore and expand on new protocols such as geospatial measurements, citizen science contributions,20 ways of generating synthetic data based on collected data,21 and forms of web scraping. AI opportunities for executing data collection, curation, and dissemination are coming.

After identifying the needs and what is feasible for collecting and disseminating data, the remaining challenges are staffing subject matter experts and managing budgeted resources. Appropriators are not responding to the costs of innovation. Small changes at the margins can be easily assessed. Entirely new protocols and methods to collect, curate, and disseminate data products need to be tested, and getting it “roughly correct” is important. The rush to implement can be costly, resulting in diminished data quality, data gaps, and loss of public trust in the official data series.22

Concluding Comments

The opportunity is at hand to reimagine a sustainable future for how USDA can meet the US agricultural economy’s data needs to inform policy and programs.

Moving forward, it is essential to assess paths that are effective (choosing the right processes and technologies) and efficient (doing the right things well). Doing business as usual is unsustainable in the face of data cancellations, massive staff losses, and budget shortfalls. With innovations, we can do the same and even more with less. But until those innovations are conceptualized and implemented, we will do less with less.

Inevitably, we need to be open to new approaches from the nonpublic sector—private firms, organizations, citizens, and nonprofit organizations. To date, the publicly provided official data are the benchmark. The federal statistical agency’s role will evolve, but it will continue to serve as the arbiter of the data that can command the public’s trust. ERS and NASS, along with the federal statistical community, must set clear expectations that future data collections are suitable and sufficient for their intended use in decision-making, planning, and operational decisions.

Data are essential to informing sound policy. Eroding access to and trust in official data compromises not only the current administration but also future administrations in crafting and implementing policy and tracking growth and prosperity in US agriculture and rural communities. Canceling data and closing off channels for external feedback lead stakeholders to rely on the historical record. This is akin to driving a car using the rearview mirror. We cannot afford to be “precisely wrong.”

About the Author

Spiro E. Stefanou is the former administrator of the US Department of Agriculture’s Economic Research Service and professor emeritus of agricultural economics at Pennsylvania State University.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Grain Stocks
Description: Issued four times yearly, contains stocks of all wheat, durum wheat, corn, sorghum, oats, barley, soybeans, flaxseed, canola, rapeseed, rye, sunflower, safflower, mustard seed, by States and U.S. and by position (on-farm or off-farm storage); includes number and capacity of off-farm storage facilities and capacity of on-farm storage facilities. The data is obtained via an off and on-farm stocks survey, the on-farm survey is a probability survey of farm operators, the off-farm stocks survey is enumerates the volume of grain in all known commercial grain storage facilities.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: USDA **Grain Stocks**

**Research checked:** October 9, 2026  
**Recommended canonical record:** [Economics, Statistics, and Market Information System — Grain Stocks](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/publication/grain-stocks)

## Executive summary

**Grain Stocks** is an active, market-sensitive statistical report published four times a year by the **National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), Agricultural Statistics Board, U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)**. It estimates quantities of grains, oilseeds, and some pulse crops held in storage on particular reference dates, distinguishing stocks stored **on farms** from those held in commercial or other **off-farm** facilities.

The description supplied in the request matches the official ESMIS description almost verbatim. It is broadly accurate, but needs several qualifications:

1. **The publication is a continuing statistical report, not a public microdata file.** It combines aggregate estimates from two confidential surveys.
2. **Not every commodity appears in every quarterly issue.** The seven major grains and oilseeds are quarterly; smaller crops, sunflower, pulses, and storage-capacity tables follow seasonal or annual schedules.
3. **The current report also includes pulse crops**—dry edible peas, lentils, and chickpeas—although these are absent from the supplied description. Rice and peanuts are excluded and covered elsewhere.
4. **Not every minor commodity is published by state.** The major commodities have state tables; several annual crops and pulse series are national only in current issues.
5. **The off-farm survey is designed as a census of the known commercial-storage frame, but it is not literally a 100-percent-response enumeration.** NASS attempts to contact all known qualifying facilities and estimates for nonresponse.
6. **Values can be revised.** Preservation and reproducible analysis therefore require release-vintage files, not only the current Quick Stats database.

The dataset is especially important because it provides one of the federal government’s principal observed measurements of U.S. crop supply between harvests. It supports supply-demand balance sheets, price discovery, farm and elevator decisions, food-security monitoring, transportation and storage planning, policy evaluation, and historical research.

---

## 1. Administrative and bibliographic profile

| Field | Information |
|---|---|
| Title | **Grain Stocks** |
| Producer | USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service |
| Official releasing body | USDA Agricultural Statistics Board |
| Archival/dissemination platform | USDA National Agricultural Library, Economics, Statistics, and Market Information System, or ESMIS |
| Status | Active and subscribable |
| Resource type in ESMIS | Report |
| Subject category | Grains and Oilseeds |
| Frequency | Four times yearly; ESMIS calls this “Seasonal” |
| Survey reference dates | March 1, June 1, September 1, December 1 |
| Normal release months | March, June, September, and January |
| ISSN | **1949-0925** |
| ESMIS publication ID | **1480** |
| ESMIS identifier | **GraiStoc** |
| Typical report filename pattern | `grstMMYY`, e.g. `grst0326` |
| Contact shown by ESMIS | nass@nass.usda.gov |
| NASS data inquiries | 800-727-9540 |
| Latest release found during this research | September 30, 2026, ESMIS release ID 796087 |
| Digital formats | PDF, plain text, ZIP; aggregate estimates also through Quick Stats web/API |
| DOI | None was exposed in the ESMIS metadata reviewed |

Useful machine-readable records:

- [ESMIS publication metadata for publication 1480](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/publication/findById/1480)
- [ESMIS release list for Grain Stocks](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/release/findByPubId/1480)
- [ESMIS public API specification](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/files/swagger/esmis_public_api.yaml)
- [Current official publication page](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/publication/grain-stocks)

The most recent release list found during this research contained a September 30, 2026 report in PDF, TXT, and ZIP form. The ESMIS API also contained three records dated September 30, 2025, apparently associated with migration or duplicate loading. A preservation program should therefore compare checksums and correction records rather than assuming that each API record is a unique issue.

---

## 2. Who produces, approves, and distributes it

### Statistical producer

The producing agency is **USDA’s National Agricultural Statistics Service**. NASS designs the samples, maintains the farm and commercial-facility frames, collects responses through its field and national operations, edits and imputes responses, and prepares state and national estimates.

### Official estimator and publisher

The report is released by the **Agricultural Statistics Board**, an internal USDA board responsible for reviewing state estimates, reconciling them to national estimates, applying commodity-balance knowledge, and approving official estimates.

This distinction matters:

- Survey respondents provide confidential information.
- NASS field offices collect and edit it.
- The Agricultural Statistics Board issues the official public estimate.
- NASS Quick Stats disseminates aggregate data.
- The National Agricultural Library’s ESMIS site preserves and distributes report files and subscriptions.

Current reports are formally approved by a designated USDA official and the Agricultural Statistics Board chairperson.

Because *Grain Stocks* is market-sensitive, NASS identifies it as a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator**. Its release is governed by controlled, preannounced procedures and the Agricultural Statistics Board’s lockup and release practices. Those procedures are intended to prevent selective early access and to give all users the same information at the scheduled time. See NASS’s description of the [Agricultural Statistics Board and lockup](https://www.nass.usda.gov/About_NASS/ASB_and_Lockup/index.php).

### Archival distributor

The **National Agricultural Library** now presents ESMIS as the archive for NASS and other USDA statistical reports. NASS methodology notices in recent years document migration from the Cornell Mann Library environment to the current NAL ESMIS platform. This platform transition is important for preservation: older Cornell URLs and newer ESMIS URLs may point to equivalent objects but have different identifiers and release records.

---

## 3. Authority, mandate, clearance, and confidentiality

### Collection and publication authority

There does not appear to be a separate statute saying “USDA shall publish a report titled *Grain Stocks*.” The series rests primarily on USDA’s broad agricultural-statistics authority.

Under [7 U.S.C. § 2204(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/7/2204), the Secretary of Agriculture is directed to procure and preserve information concerning agriculture, including through “the collection of statistics.” NASS performs this function for USDA. This general authority is also the historical basis for the Agricultural Survey Records system.

NASS’s mission is to provide meaningful, accurate, and objective agricultural statistics in service to U.S. agriculture and rural communities. *Grain Stocks* is part of that ongoing statistical program, not a one-time regulatory collection.

### Paperwork Reduction Act clearance

Federal surveys require Office of Management and Budget clearance. NASS’s methodology explains that it must demonstrate:

- a public need for the information,
- sound statistical practice,
- that equivalent data are not already available elsewhere, and
- that respondent burden is not excessive.

The current off-farm questionnaire displays:

- **OMB control number 0535-0007**
- approval expiration: **June 30, 2028**
- project code: **125**
- estimated average completion time: **15 minutes**

See, for example, the [December 2025 off-farm Grain Stocks questionnaire](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Methodology_and_Data_Quality/Grain_Stocks/02_2026/IL_Off_Farm_GrainStocks_Questionnaire_Dec2025.pdf).

The companion on-farm Agricultural Survey has its own questionnaire and current OMB display. It should not be assumed that the off-farm control number covers every component of the report.

### Voluntary response

Response is **voluntary**, even though the off-farm survey is a census in statistical design. “Census” here means NASS attempts to survey the entire known eligible frame; it does not mean response is legally mandatory.

### Confidentiality

Individual farm and facility responses are confidential statistical information. The relevant protections include:

- [7 U.S.C. § 2276](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/7/2276), which generally restricts use and disclosure to aggregate statistical forms that do not identify the respondent;
- the **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act**, Title III of Pub. L. 115-435, codified in 44 U.S.C. chapter 35; and
- NASS confidentiality and security pledges.

NASS’s [Grain Stocks survey guide](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Surveys/Guide_to_NASS_Surveys/Off-Farm_Grain_Stocks/) states that information is used for statistical purposes only and may not be disclosed in identifiable form to anyone other than authorized employees or agents. Willful disclosure carries criminal penalties.

The practical effects are:

- facility-level and farm-level microdata are not public;
- published state cells may be marked **(D)** when publication could disclose an individual operation;
- “off-farm census” does not imply a public list of every facility and its inventory;
- FOIA should not be expected to yield identifiable respondent records.

The USDA privacy-system notice for Agricultural Survey Records cites 7 U.S.C. 2204, 7 U.S.C. 2276, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and CIPSEA, and says respondent records are retained and disposed of under approved National Archives and Records Administration schedules.

### Information quality and scientific integrity

The program is also subject to federal statistical information-quality requirements, OMB statistical standards, and NASS scientific-integrity policies. NASS documents the methods and quality measures separately from the quarterly report, allowing users to distinguish the estimate from the process that produced it.

---

## 4. Historical development

### Broader agricultural-statistics lineage

NASS traces its institutional roots to USDA’s Division of Statistics in 1863. USDA issued its first crop report that year. The Crop Reporting Board was created in 1905; it developed into today’s Agricultural Statistics Board. A 1961 reorganization created the Statistical Reporting Service, the predecessor of NASS. See [NASS’s history of agricultural statistics](https://www.nass.usda.gov/About_NASS/History_of_Ag_Statistics/).

### Direct serial lineage

| Period | Publication |
|---|---|
| 1943–1973 | **Stocks of Grains** |
| 1974–present | **Grain Stocks** |

ESMIS describes [*Stocks of Grains*](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/publication/findById/157) as a quarterly publication produced from 1943 through 1973, containing crop carryover, remaining grain stocks, and on- and off-farm storage-facility information. In 1974, the content continued under the title *Grain Stocks*.

The current ESMIS *Grain Stocks* collection contains a transitional record dated October 24, 1973 and a regular run beginning in 1974. Researchers constructing a long series should catalog the predecessor and successor as related but distinct serials, even when analytically chaining their estimates.

### Related historical products

- [**Producer Owned Grain Stocks**](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/publication/findById/71): a related annual publication covering 1979–1982 for producer-owned corn, wheat, sorghum, and soybean stocks.
- [**Stocks of Grains, Oilseeds, and Hay — Final Estimates**](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/publication/findById/48): revised/final benchmark publications whose ESMIS holdings cover periods from 1949–1955 through 2008–2013.
- [**Historical Track Record — Grain Stocks**](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/publication/findById/58): annual historical evaluation files issued from 2003 through 2011.
- [**Price Reaction after Crop Reports**](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/publication/search?query=Grain%20Stocks): an active historical series documenting commodity-price responses following Crop Production and Grain Stocks releases.

### Digital-publication history

Older issues are generally scanned PDFs. More recent issues are born-digital and available as PDF, fixed-width plain text, and ZIP packages. The archival platform has also changed, with older USDA/Cornell ESMIS URLs giving way to the current NAL ESMIS site. Consequently, a durable citation should include the title, reference date, release date, publication ID, release ID, file name, and access date—not merely a bare URL.

---

## 5. Subject scope and publication schedule

### What “stocks” means

A stock is the estimated quantity of a commodity physically on hand at the reference date. It is a point-in-time quantity, not a measure of production or consumption during the quarter.

The reports also calculate **indicated disappearance**, an inferred measure obtained through the commodity balance sheet. Disappearance is not a separately measured consumption survey.

### Position

The two basic positions are:

- **On farms:** whole grains and oilseeds stored on the farm operation, whether intended for feed, seed, sale, or a government program.
- **Off farms:** stocks at commercial or nonfarm facilities, including mills, elevators, warehouses, terminals, and processors.

“Position” describes storage location, not necessarily ownership. The off-farm questionnaire includes grain in the facility regardless of whether it belongs to farmers, elevators, processors, the Commodity Credit Corporation, or another owner. It includes domestic and imported whole grain, seed grain, bulk and sacked storage, and temporary piles. It excludes grain that the reporting company owns but has stored at another licensed elevator.

### Reference and release cycle

| Reference date | Normal release | Main contents |
|---|---|---|
| December 1 | Early January, with the Crop Production Annual Summary | Major quarterly commodities; prior-period revisions; annual-crop revisions; pulse stocks; on-farm storage capacity; number and capacity of off-farm storage facilities |
| March 1 | End of March | Major quarterly commodities, sunflower, and previous-quarter revisions |
| June 1 | End of June | Major commodities, flaxseed, canola, rapeseed, rye, pulse crops, and previous-quarter revisions |
| September 1 | End of September | Major commodities, sunflower, safflower, mustard seed, revisions, and in some years revised corn and soybean acreage, yield, and production |

The [NASS survey guide](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Surveys/Guide_to_NASS_Surveys/Off-Farm_Grain_Stocks/) provides the current seasonal breakdown.

### Commodity coverage

#### Core quarterly grains and oilseeds

- all wheat
- durum wheat, shown as a detail within all wheat
- corn
- sorghum
- oats
- barley
- soybeans

These are the principal series with U.S. and state tables by on-farm, off-farm, and total positions.

#### Seasonal, annual, or smaller crops

- flaxseed
- canola
- rapeseed
- rye
- sunflower, normally March and September and broken into oil and non-oil types
- safflower
- mustard seed
- dry edible peas
- lentils
- chickpeas, including large and small classes

The January issue includes revised annual-crop data and the storage-capacity tables. The current [January 2026 report](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/release-files/795726/grst0126.txt) illustrates the full annual structure.

### Important correction to the supplied description

The supplied text implies that all listed commodities are available by state. That is not how current issues are organized:

- the major commodity tables are “States and United States”;
- annual-crop tables and pulse tables are generally “United States” only;
- sunflower is published by state and type in the relevant issues;
- facility tables are by state and United States.

Thus, the official high-level ESMIS description is accurate as a series-level summary, but it should not be interpreted as promising state-level detail for every commodity in every issue.

### Geographic level

Published estimates are principally:

- United States
- states
- some regional groupings, such as New England

They are **not county-level** and do not publish facility coordinates. Suppressed state values are aggregated into an **Unallocated** line so the U.S. total can still be published.

### Units

- major grains and oilseeds: generally thousand bushels in domestic tables and metric tons in metric tables
- sunflower: pounds
- pulses: hundredweight
- storage capacity: bushels
- off-farm facilities: number of facilities and capacity

The report includes domestic and metric U.S. tables.

---

## 6. Data-collection methodology

The current methodology is documented in NASS’s [Grain Stocks Methodology and Quality Measures](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Methodology_and_Data_Quality/Grain_Stocks/index.php), including the [February 2026 edition](https://data.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Methodology_and_Data_Quality/Grain_Stocks/02_2026/gsq0226.pdf).

### Two-source design

The published estimate combines:

1. the **Agricultural Survey**, measuring on-farm stocks and storage; and
2. the **Off-Farm Grain Stocks survey**, measuring commercial/nonfarm stocks and storage.

The two are combined after separate review and estimation.

### On-farm Agricultural Survey

The Agricultural Survey is conducted quarterly in all states except Hawaii. Its target population is farms with cropland and/or storage capacity.

NASS uses a **dual-frame probability design**:

- a list frame of known farms; and
- an area frame that identifies farms not adequately represented on the list frame, called the nonoverlap portion.

List-frame records are screened for planted acres or storage capacity. Some states use lower population boundaries, such as 50 acres of cropland or 1,000 bushels of grain-storage capacity. The area-frame component helps preserve coverage of farms missing from the list.

The list sample is selected using a **multivariate probability-proportional-to-size** design. Sample weights are calibrated so weighted sample measures agree with the list-frame totals for selected commodities. NASS also uses replicates and stocks panels to reduce respondent burden and measure quarter-to-quarter change from the same operations.

As an issue-specific example, the September 2025 report described an on-farm probability sample of approximately **55,700 farm operators**. Sample size varies by quarter and year.

### Off-Farm Grain Stocks survey

The Off-Farm Grain Stocks survey is conducted quarterly in all states except Alaska, Connecticut, Hawaii, Nevada, and Rhode Island.

Its target population includes U.S. entities capable of storing at least **1,000 bushels** of eligible grain or oilseeds off the farm, such as:

- elevators,
- warehouses,
- terminals,
- grain and oilseed processing plants, and
- other qualifying commercial storage facilities.

Rice and peanuts are excluded. Rice has a separate NASS report.

The survey is a **census of the known frame**, not a probability sample. Stratification is used for nonresponse adjustment. In the September 2025 issue, NASS reported approximately:

- **7,900 facilities**, and
- **11.8 billion bushels of storage capacity**.

Reports are normally received from operations representing about **90 percent of capacity**; estimates are made for missing facilities to complete the frame.

### Data-collection period

The reference date is the first of March, June, September, or December. Data collection normally lasts about 15 calendar days and may begin slightly before the reference date. Regional field offices edit and analyze their data, after which the Agricultural Statistics Board performs national review and prepares official estimates.

December 1 data are released in January rather than at the end of December.

### Estimation and balancing

NASS uses direct expansions and ratio estimators for the on-farm data and nonresponse/imputation procedures for both sources. Survey results are reviewed for:

- reasonableness,
- consistency with prior estimates,
- current crop size,
- state-to-national coherence, and
- commodity-balance relationships.

After on- and off-farm estimates are combined, NASS uses a **balance-sheet check** involving production, imports, exports, crushings, millings, feed and residual use, and other recorded uses. This helps identify implausible estimates but does not turn the result into an exact accounting count.

---

## 7. Data quality, uncertainty, and revisions

### Sampling error

Only the on-farm component is a probability sample, so it is subject to sampling error. The off-farm component is a frame census and does not have the same form of sampling variability, although it still has coverage and response errors.

NASS’s methodology gives target U.S. coefficients of variation, varying by quarter and commodity, of approximately:

- 2–4 percent for corn,
- 2–5 percent for soybeans, and
- 3–4 percent for all wheat.

Over roughly the preceding decade, reported U.S. survey CVs ranged approximately:

- 1.5–4.4 percent for corn,
- 1.7–7.5 percent for soybeans, and
- 2.3–5.0 percent for all wheat.

State-level uncertainty is generally higher because state samples are smaller.

The September 2025 report provided these relative standard errors:

- corn: 4.2 percent
- soybeans: 6.0 percent
- all wheat: 3.2 percent
- sorghum: 15.5 percent
- barley: 7.3 percent
- oats: 6.2 percent

For the first three, NASS interpreted these as approximate 95-percent ranges of ±8.4 percent for corn, ±12.0 percent for soybeans, and ±6.4 percent for all wheat.

### Non-sampling error

Both components are subject to:

- frame omissions or duplication,
- inaccurate respondent reporting,
- recording and processing mistakes,
- nonresponse,
- imputation error, and
- inconsistent interpretation of stocks or capacity.

NASS minimizes these through questionnaire design, editing, quality controls, state and national review, and balance-sheet checks, but they cannot be measured directly in the same way as sampling error.

### Revisions

Estimates are not immutable. Later quarterly and January issues can revise earlier values when survey, production, export, administrative, or balance-sheet information changes.

A clear example:

- The initial [September 30, 2025 report](https://release.nass.usda.gov/reports/grst0925.txt) estimated September 1 corn stocks at **1,531,613 thousand bushels**, including **888,413 thousand off farms**.
- The [January 12, 2026 report](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/release-files/795726/grst0126.txt) revised the same September 1 estimates to **1,551,286 thousand total**, including **908,086 thousand off farms**.

Anyone reproducing what the market knew on September 30 must use the September release, not silently substitute the revised January value.

### Disclosure controls

Report symbols include:

- **(D):** withheld to avoid disclosing an individual operation
- **(NA):** not available
- **Unallocated:** state values withheld for disclosure reasons or minor producing states not separately published

`(D)` does not mean zero. State rows should not be summed naively without accounting for the unallocated line.

### Comparability cautions

- All wheat includes durum wheat; do not add durum to all wheat as though it were a separate total.
- Commodity coverage varies by issue.
- Historical state publication patterns can change.
- Marketing years differ among crops.
- Storage capacity is generally multipurpose capacity, not commodity-specific capacity.
- “Indicated disappearance” is a residual balance measure, not a direct utilization observation.
- Values are estimates as of one date and may be strongly seasonal.
- Current Quick Stats records do not provide full sampling-error columns for every estimate.

---

## 8. Access routes and data structure

### 1. ESMIS report archive

Best for:

- official release-vintage documents,
- long-term publication history,
- PDF/TXT/ZIP preservation,
- subscriptions,
- publication and release metadata.

The ESMIS REST API is read-only and does not require an API key. It supports agency, publication, and release lookup. Its release objects provide direct file URLs.

Important distinction: the ESMIS API supplies **report metadata and files**, not a normalized grain-stocks observation table.

### 2. NASS Quick Stats

Best for:

- interactive filtering,
- CSV extraction,
- programmatic time-series construction,
- combining stocks with acreage, yield, production, prices, and other NASS series.

The [Quick Stats API documentation](https://quickstats.nass.usda.gov/api) explains that:

- a free API key is required;
- output formats are JSON, CSV, or XML;
- `/api/api_GET` returns data;
- `/api/get_counts` tests whether a query exceeds the 50,000-record limit;
- `/api/get_param_values` discovers valid parameter values;
- bulk files are available when a query would exceed the API limit.

Representative columns include:

- `source_desc`
- `sector_desc`
- `group_desc`
- `commodity_desc`
- `class_desc`
- `statisticcat_desc`
- `unit_desc`
- `short_desc`
- `domain_desc`
- `domaincat_desc`
- `agg_level_desc`
- state ANSI, abbreviation, and name
- `year`
- `freq_desc`
- `reference_period_desc`
- `load_time`
- `Value`

A query pattern for exploring corn stocks might be:

```text
https://quickstats.nass.usda.gov/api/api_GET/
?key=YOUR_API_KEY
&source_desc=SURVEY
&sector_desc=CROPS
&commodity_desc=CORN
&statisticcat_desc=STOCKS
&agg_level_desc=STATE
&year__GE=2020
&format=CSV
```

Before relying on the exact parameters, use `get_param_values` and inspect `short_desc`. On-farm and off-farm position may be encoded in the data-item description rather than exposed as a clean standalone variable.

### 3. Quick Stats bulk downloads

The [NASS datasets page](https://www.nass.usda.gov/datasets/) provides larger Quick Stats extracts. These are preferable to repeatedly calling the API when building a national longitudinal database.

A preservationist should record the extract date and source file because Quick Stats is a living database, not an immutable issue archive.

### 4. Report ZIP packages

Current ESMIS issues offer ZIP packages in addition to PDF and TXT. A repository should inventory and document the ZIP contents rather than assuming they contain either a full database extract or merely duplicate presentation files.

---

## 9. Typical users and why they use it

### Farmers, producer organizations, and lenders

Users compare current stocks with prior years, judge how much old-crop supply remains, and assess marketing and storage decisions. Lenders and cooperatives use state and national conditions for credit and operational planning.

### Grain elevators, merchandisers, processors, and logistics firms

These users monitor:

- whether supply is concentrated on farms or in commercial channels,
- likely farmer selling pressure,
- storage occupancy and future capacity needs,
- rail, barge, and trucking demand, and
- procurement risks.

### Commodity traders and market analysts

*Grain Stocks* is a recognized market-moving report. It helps traders recalibrate old-crop supply, disappearance, and expected ending stocks. NASS’s own *Price Reaction after Crop Reports* series exists precisely because these releases can affect corn, soybean, wheat, and cotton prices.

### USDA economists and forecasters

The World Agricultural Outlook Board, Economic Research Service, and other USDA analysts use the estimates in supply-demand balance sheets.

For example, the July 2025 [ERS Feed Outlook](https://downloads.usda.library.cornell.edu/usda-esmis/files/44558d29f/xs55pc373/8k71qg608/FDS-25g.pdf) used the June *Grain Stocks* report to revise corn disappearance, 2024/25 ending stocks, 2025/26 carry-in, feed and residual use, exports, and supply forecasts.

### Federal, state, and congressional policymakers

Uses include:

- monitoring food and feed supply,
- assessing farm-program conditions,
- evaluating disaster and transportation stress,
- studying storage infrastructure,
- supporting budget and oversight decisions, and
- grounding agricultural legislation in consistent national estimates.

### Academics and data scientists

Research applications include:

- supply-demand and price modeling,
- commodity-market event studies,
- storage-behavior analysis,
- seasonal and spatial agricultural economics,
- infrastructure and resilience research, and
- long-run structural change in U.S. agriculture.

### Journalists and civil-society organizations

The data provide an independent baseline for reporting on:

- food supply,
- crop shortages or surpluses,
- rural infrastructure,
- supply-chain stress,
- drought and disaster effects, and
- market volatility.

---

## 10. Benefits to the public

### A common, trusted measurement

The report gives farmers, companies, journalists, researchers, and agencies the same official supply baseline. Without it, large commercial actors would have a greater informational advantage because they could build proprietary storage and merchandising estimates unavailable to the public.

### Better price discovery

Timely stock estimates reduce uncertainty about remaining supply and help markets price grain and oilseeds more efficiently. The preannounced, embargoed release process also reduces the risk of selective leaks.

### Supply-chain and food-security monitoring

Four observations per year show how stocks move from harvest through the marketing year. This helps policymakers and emergency planners identify unusually tight or abundant supplies.

### Infrastructure planning

The January facility and capacity tables support state and national analysis of commercial and farm storage capacity, although they are not sufficiently detailed for facility-level resilience planning.

### Public accountability and research

The long archive allows independent evaluation of commodity programs, market concentration narratives, price volatility, production shocks, and policy outcomes. The publication of methodology, survey forms, quality measures, corrections, and historical track records strengthens scientific accountability.

### Efficiency of shared statistical infrastructure

Individual firms could estimate some of this information privately, but a public series avoids duplicative collection and creates a uniform reference that small farms, local governments, journalists, and researchers could not otherwise afford.

## 11. Preservation guidance

### Treat each quarterly report as a release vintage

Preserve, for every issue:

- canonical landing page,
- PDF,
- TXT,
- ZIP,
- release timestamp,
- reference date,
- release ID and publication ID,
- ESMIS API JSON response,
- checksums for every file,
- release-calendar entry,
- any correction or Agricultural Statistics Board notice.

The file as first released and the later revised value in Quick Stats are different information objects.

### Preserve methodological context with the data

At minimum, archive annually:

- the current Methodology and Quality Measures report;
- Agricultural Survey questionnaire;
- off-farm Grain Stocks questionnaire;
- OMB control number and expiration;
- reliability statements;
- relevant executive briefings;
- correction logs;
- NASS notices about schedule changes or program changes.

Without these files, a future user may not know whether a change is a real supply shift, a frame redesign, a questionnaire change, or a revision.

### Preserve both report and database snapshots

Recommended practice is to keep:

1. the immutable quarterly report as issued; and
2. a dated Quick Stats query or bulk extract used for analysis.

Quick Stats is authoritative and convenient, but it is a current database. Its `load_time` is useful provenance, but it is not a substitute for preserving the original release.

### Check for platform migration and duplicates

The archive’s movement from Cornell-based hosting to NAL ESMIS creates multiple identifiers and URL families. The API’s duplicate September 2025 records demonstrate why preservation systems should:

- calculate hashes,
- retain HTTP response metadata,
- record redirect chains,
- review NASS correction logs, and
- distinguish migration duplicates from substantive corrections.

### File-format recommendations

- Retain the original PDF and TXT as primary evidence.
- Convert PDF to PDF/A only as a derivative, not as a replacement.
- For scanned historical PDFs, retain the scan and any OCR layer separately.
- Parse fixed-width TXT into a documented tidy format, but preserve the source text unchanged.
- Inventory ZIP packages and calculate checksums for both the package and extracted members.
- Use WARC or equivalent web archiving for the publication page and API response.

### Suggested preservation metadata

```text
Title: Grain Stocks
Creator: National Agricultural Statistics Service
Issuing body: Agricultural Statistics Board, USDA
Reference date: [March/June/September/December 1, YYYY]
Release date: [actual release date]
Publication ID: 1480
Publication identifier: GraiStoc
Release ID: [ESMIS ID]
ISSN: 1949-0925
Geography: United States and states
Position: on-farm; off-farm; all positions
Commodity: [commodity and class/type]
Unit: [1,000 bushels; metric tons; pounds; cwt]
Source surveys: Agricultural Survey; Off-Farm Grain Stocks survey
OMB clearance: [component-specific number and expiration]
File URL and SHA-256 checksum
Access date
Revision/correction status
```

### Rights

Published USDA reports are generally U.S. government works in the public domain in the United States under 17 U.S.C. §105. Users should still provide attribution and should separately review terms for any third-party platform, repackaged database, image, or non-federal contribution. Respondent microdata are not public-domain data; they are protected confidential records.

## 12. Data-librarian guidance

### Cataloging interpretation

Catalog *Grain Stocks* both as:

- a continuing statistical serial, and
- a source from which recurring aggregate datasets are extracted.

Do not merge the predecessor and successor without a relationship note:

- predecessor: *Stocks of Grains*, 1943–1973
- successor: *Grain Stocks*, 1974–present

Useful subject terms include:

- grain—storage—United States—statistics
- oilseeds—storage—United States—statistics
- grain stocks
- agricultural estimates
- farm storage
- grain elevators
- food supply
- United States—states—statistics
- periodic statistical reports

### Citation practice

For a report issue:

> U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Statistics Service, Agricultural Statistics Board. *Grain Stocks* [reference date]. Released [release date]. ISSN 1949-0925. ESMIS publication 1480, release [release ID]. [URL].

For a database extraction:

> U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Statistics Service. “Grain Stocks.” Quick Stats database, query parameters [list parameters], accessed [date]. Values and `load_time` recorded [date].

### Discovery gaps

The ESMIS API is useful, but its release metadata may leave bibliographic citation and temporal-coverage fields blank. Libraries should enrich local metadata with:

- reference date,
- release date,
- commodity schedule,
- revision relationships,
- predecessor/successor relationships,
- format,
- checksum,
- and issue-level URL.

## 13. Data-science guidance

### Recommended analytical workflow

1. Choose whether the goal is:
   - current official estimates, or
   - point-in-time information as originally released.
2. For current estimates, use Quick Stats and record `load_time`.
3. For market-history or forecast evaluation, use ESMIS release-vintage files.
4. Normalize commodity, class/type, geography, reference date, position, unit, and value.
5. Preserve source-release ID and original text value.
6. Track revisions by comparing the same reference date across later releases.
7. Join with production, acreage, trade, crush, and price series only after aligning crop marketing years.

### Suggested tidy schema

```text
commodity
commodity_class_or_type
reference_date
release_date
release_id
geography_level
geography_name
state_fips
position
value
unit
suppression_flag
availability_flag
revision_flag
quickstats_load_time
source_file
source_file_hash
```

### Common engineering problems

- `Value` may contain thousands separators or nonnumeric availability codes.
- On/off position may be embedded in `short_desc`.
- State and U.S. observations have different aggregation levels.
- `(D)` is not zero.
- “Unallocated” is a real reconciliation category, not a place.
- Durum wheat is part of all wheat.
- Sunflower and pulse units differ from the major grains.
- Reference period and year must be combined to form a true date.
- Some current-quarter cells are blank until that estimation period begins.
- State-published cells can change between issues.
- The current database may contain a revised value rather than the initially released value.

### Uncertainty modeling

Do not assume that the national CV for one commodity or quarter applies to another state, commodity, or period. The report publishes selected reliability measures, while Quick Stats generally provides point estimates rather than a complete variance dataset. Researchers needing formal uncertainty should consult the current methodology and avoid inventing state-level standard errors.

## 14. Policy-activist assessment

### What this dataset can support

- National and state food-supply monitoring
- Analysis of on-farm versus commercial storage dependence
- Seasonal supply-chain stress analysis
- Evaluation of whether storage capacity is keeping pace with production
- Accountability reporting on agricultural markets and federal policy
- Historical research on surpluses, shortages, farm programs, and market shocks
- Independent scrutiny of government supply forecasts

### What it cannot establish by itself

- corporate ownership or control of storage facilities;
- facility-level resilience, location, or closure risk;
- county-level shortages;
- the identity of grain owners;
- final use by food, feed, seed, export, or fuel;
- commodity quality, moisture, or condition;
- prices, transportation costs, or market concentration;
- real-time conditions between quarterly reference dates.

For competition, consolidation, emergency-management, or community-resilience research, it must be supplemented with warehouse licensing, transportation, corporate, disaster, price, and local infrastructure data.

### Policy tradeoff

Confidentiality encourages accurate reporting from farms and commercial facilities and is legally central to the statistical system. The cost is reduced public visibility into individual facilities and some small-state cells. Policy analysis should respect that tradeoff rather than treating suppressed values as agency opacity or as evidence of zero supply.

### Advocacy and improvement opportunities

Useful requests to USDA and NASS include:

- continued stable funding for frame maintenance and both surveys;
- preservation of Agricultural Statistics Board independence and scheduled releases;
- stable, machine-readable quarterly files;
- explicit position variables rather than position embedded in text descriptions;
- release-vintage APIs and correction feeds;
- persistent identifiers and checksums;
- clearer documentation of ZIP contents;
- more complete uncertainty metadata;
- careful expansion of non-disclosive regional storage-capacity detail;
- long-term preservation of methodology and questionnaires with every release.

| Loss of report vintage through reliance on current Quick Stats | High | Later revisions can overwrite the value needed for reproducibility |
| Platform migration and duplicate records | Medium | Cornell-to-NAL migration has created multiple URLs and duplicate API records |
| Scanned historical PDFs | Medium | OCR and table extraction may be unreliable |
| Methodology separated from data | Medium | Future users may lack sampling, frame, and revision context |

| Confidential microdata unavailable | Structural | Estimates cannot be independently recomputed from respondent-level records |
| Commodity schedule misunderstood | Medium | Users may assume every listed crop is quarterly and state-level |
| Survey/program discontinuation or schedule disruption | Low-to-medium | The series is active and economically important, but government schedules can change; ASB notices should be monitored |

## Bottom line

*Grain Stocks* is one of USDA’s most consequential recurring agricultural datasets: a quarterly, state-and-national estimate of how much of the U.S. crop supply remains in storage and where it is positioned in the marketing system. Its value comes from the combination of a probability-based on-farm survey, an attempted census of commercial storage, Agricultural Statistics Board review, scheduled market-sensitive release, and an archive extending through a predecessor series to 1943.

For preservation, the central rule is to **preserve the report as a dated statistical event**, not merely the latest numbers. For analysis, the central rule is to **normalize commodity, position, geography, reference date, unit, release vintage, and revision status**. For policy, the central limitation is that the series provides authoritative aggregate supply and capacity signals but not facility-level transparency.

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone:**  
  Not applicable under the rubric.

- **High Risk:**  
  There is no statute specifically requiring a quarterly report titled *Grain Stocks*. The legal authority is the broad directive in [7 U.S.C. § 2204](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/7/2204) for the Secretary of Agriculture to procure, preserve, and distribute agricultural information through statistics. Private commodity-analysis firms could theoretically produce partial substitutes.

- **Moderate Risk:**  
  The program is not specifically named in statute, but it has clear governmental uses:
  - The 2025 Federal Register notice calls the Stocks Reports an OMB-defined **Principal Federal Economic Indicator**.
  - It says USDA uses stocks statistics to administer programs, while states, producers, buyers, and market participants use them for marketing and policy purposes.
  - The 2026 Agricultural Surveys notice says crop and grain-storage statistics support federal and state programs involving conservation, foreign trade, school meals, education, and related activities.
  - No other public federal collection provides the same quarterly combination of major commodities, state detail, on-farm/off-farm position, and commercial-storage capacity. The five-year Census of Agriculture is not a quarterly substitute.

- **No Known Issue:**  
  The statutory citation is explicit and stable, but it is general agricultural-statistics authority rather than a detailed mandate specifying this report’s commodities, frequency, geography, or publication deadline.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

The broad authority is real and the public-program use is well documented, but the dataset is not itself specifically required by statute. No equally comprehensive public substitute is known.

  - The American Statistical Association estimates NASS lost approximately **41 percent** of its FY 2024 staffing.
  - AEI’s former ERS administrator reports a **40 percent** NASS staff loss during FY 2025.
  - USDA’s FY 2027 explanatory notes report a reduction from 754 to 489 staff, approximately 35 percent.
  - The American Statistical Association reports that, as of mid-2026, three of five NASS office-director positions were vacant or acting and five of seven division directors were acting.
  - USDA is relocating positions and offering separation incentives, creating the possibility of additional attrition.
  - The permanent NASS administrator has not been reported as removed, and the budget cut is far below 20 percent, but the staffing-loss threshold alone supports High Risk.

- **Moderate Risk:**  
  USDA’s narrower official staff-count series shows a reduction of approximately 35 percent, which independently falls in the rubric’s 10–39 percent range. The nominal FY 2026 request of $185 million was only about 1.5 percent below the FY 2025 enacted $187.85 million, although independent analyses estimate larger purchasing-power losses over several years.

- **No Known Issue:**  
  Nominal funding has not been cut by 10 percent, reports remain on schedule, and NASS retains a permanent administrator. Those facts would support a lower rating if considered alone, but they do not offset the documented staffing losses.

- **USAJobs tracker caveat:**  
  The tracker shows USDA job postings declining from 10,466 in 2024 to 1,482 in 2025, an approximately 86 percent reduction. This is not NASS-specific and job listings are not hires, so it should not be used as a staffing count. It is nevertheless consistent with the reported contraction in federal recruitment.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

The rubric uses “and/or.” Independent estimates of a 40–41 percent staff loss place the category in High Risk even though USDA’s narrower staff-count series is closer to 35 percent and the budget cut itself is modest.

## 6. Policy

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone:**  
  No evidence that *Grain Stocks* has been terminated.

- **High Risk:**  
  There are significant administration-driven changes elsewhere at NASS:
  - USDA’s FY 2026 budget proposed eliminating the Farm Labor Report.
  - The NASS Advisory Committee on Agriculture Statistics was disbanded in 2025.
  - USDA is reorganizing and relocating statistical-agency staff.
  - USDA is undertaking a broad review that could consolidate reports.  
  However, I found no presidential-action-driven replacement ICR for *Grain Stocks*, no negative warning on the dataset page, and no implemented policy change eliminating or reducing this particular report.

- **Moderate Risk:**  
  There are explicit pending or proposed changes:
  - USDA announced a NASS modernization plan focused on reporting systems, transparency, response rates, and confidence in the data.
  - Secretary Rollins specifically referred to *Grain Stocks* when discussing response-rate declines and report revisions.
  - She also suggested USDA would examine whether all of its hundreds of reports remain necessary.
  - The March 2026 ICR changes the Agricultural Surveys Program by increasing the Grain Stocks-related sample, reinstating a coverage-evaluation survey, and updating race/ethnicity standards. Those changes are pending or recently implemented but do not reduce the published dataset.

- **No Known Issue:**  
  The report’s frequency and published content have remained intact, and the most directly relevant ICR change increases rather than reduces collection. If only the dataset itself were considered, there has been no demonstrated policy-driven reduction.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

There is no implemented adverse change to *Grain Stocks*, but USDA leadership has announced a pending review and possible report consolidation. That squarely fits the rubric’s category for proposed changes or official statements indicating that changes are being considered.

---

## Overall interpretation

The **near-term risk of the historical reports disappearing or the quarterly series immediately stopping appears low**. The deeper risk is institutional: NASS has experienced severe staffing losses, leadership vacancies, declining survey response, forced relocation, and an announced review of its statistical portfolio. Those conditions make future degradation or consolidation substantially more plausible than the currently uninterrupted publication record alone would suggest.

Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**  
Future Data Availability: **No Known Issue**  
Data Quality: **Moderate Risk**

Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**
